entry.title: Report, October 19, 2026
Shopify yearly prices: Grow shows $79 or $89/mo, Advanced $299 or $359/mo (price test)
entry.summary: Shopify's pricing page is showing visitors two different pay-yearly prices for the same plans. On October 19, 2026, ten back-to-back checks of shopify.com/pricing returned Grow at $79/mo and Advanced at $299/mo six times, and Grow at $89/mo and Advanced at $359/mo four times. Pay-monthly prices were the same in every version ($105/mo for Grow, $399/mo for Advanced), and Basic stayed at $29/mo yearly and $39/mo monthly. Our daily snapshots showed the higher $89/$359 yearly prices every morning from October 15 through 18 and the older $79/$299 prices again today, so the higher prices look like a price test shown to some visitors, not a completed price increase. Over a year, the gap is $120 on Grow ($948 vs $1,068) and $720 on Advanced ($3,588 vs $4,308).

entry.title: USPS rule (Oct 19, 2026): senders billed for unpaid foreign duties on packages, even if disputed, 6% interest
entry.summary: The U.S. Postal Service published an interim final rule in the Federal Register on October 19, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-21310, "Customs Requirements and Payment Procedures for Certain Customs Charges") that took effect the same day. It rewrites the International Mail Manual so the person who mails a package abroad can be billed later for the destination country's duties, taxes and import fees. A new section 424, "Unpaid Destination Customs Charges," says that if a customs authority, postal operator or broker in the destination country "seeks to collect duties, taxes, or import fees from the mailer or the Postal Service" and they "have not been paid in full, the Postal Service (or its representative) will send an invoice to the mailer for such amounts." The mailer "must pay the Postal Service ... the entire amount due in accordance with the invoice terms, even if the mailer disputes the assessment," and is not relieved of the charge "regardless of whether the item is delivered, lost, damaged, or returned." Late payment accrues "interest ... at a rate of 6 percent per annum," and USPS can recover its collection costs and may treat the unpaid amount as a postage revenue deficiency. You can dispute only USPS accounting errors. Any challenge to the foreign charge itself "must be addressed directly to such party without involvement from the Postal Service," and USPS says it "is not responsible for the accuracy" of those charges. The rule also says that where a destination country requires a delivered duty paid (DDP) shipment, "the mailer must send the mailpiece on a delivered duty paid basis," and that duties and fees "are not included in the postage paid by the mailer." USPS says the trigger is the European Union ending its de minimis exemption for most low-value goods on July 1, 2026. Under the new EU rules, some EU postal operators require prepaid duties, charge fees when customs data is wrong, or go after the sender when the recipient doesn't pay. USPS's own prepaid-duties page says EU countries now charge a flat, nonrefundable €3 duty on merchandise up to €150 and on gifts worth over €45 up to €150, and that USPS Delivered Duty Paid is built into retail counters and Click-N-Ship. The rule text itself isn't limited to the EU: it applies wherever a destination party seeks unpaid charges. USPS is taking comments until November 18, 2026. Coverage so far (checked October 19): a legal-news summary (LexVira), a personal-finance blog (Main Street Dollars) and a small online outlet (The Digital Free Press). We found no major news outlet reporting it. What it replaces (checked October 19, 2026): the International Mail Manual still posted on USPS's Postal Explorer site hasn't been updated yet. Its section 131.34 says "No provision is made for prepayment of customs duty on mail addressed for delivery in foreign countries," that "most countries will collect from the recipient," and that duties and fees "are not included in the postage paid by the mailer." It has no section 424 and doesn't mention invoicing the sender. How private carriers compare: FedEx's duties-and-taxes page says that if the recipient refuses the package or refuses to pay, "the original shipper will be billed for duties and taxes." UPS tells shippers "if the receiver does not pay, UPS may recover the outstanding amounts from you." DHL Express's Terms and Conditions of Carriage say the shipper "shall pay or reimburse DHL for all Customs Duties and other charges ... if Consignee has failed to pay." So USPS is moving toward how commercial carriers already work. Its version goes further in writing: pay "even if the mailer disputes the assessment," keep owing it if the item is lost or returned, 6% interest, and disputes limited to USPS accounting errors. What you can do before you mail: prepay with USPS Delivered Duty Paid. It's available only at the time of mailing, on Priority Mail Express International, Priority Mail International and First-Class Package International Service, through a retail counter, Click-N-Ship, USPS APIs or Global Shipping Software, and only to select countries. USPS's July 1, 2026 Postal Bulletin added 21 destinations, mostly EU countries and territories, including France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands. Describe each item accurately on the customs form, because USPS uses the descriptions to assign HS codes and charges the €3 duty "for each unique HS Code." The European Commission says the €3 applies per item type (one T-shirt plus one watch is €6), that the seller or importer is normally the one who pays, and that product identifiers become mandatory on November 1, 2026. Etsy's help center recommends DDP shipping to reduce "refused shipments, and unexpected charges at delivery." eBay sellers using eBay International Shipping send items to a U.S. hub instead, and eBay says import fees are collected from the buyer at checkout or on delivery. How to comment: this is an interim final rule, so it's already in force, but USPS is taking comments until November 18, 2026. The Federal Register notice says to email PCFederalRegister@usps.gov with the subject line "Customs Requirements and Payment Procedures" and your name and address, or mail comments to the Manager of Product Classification, U.S. Postal Service, 475 L'Enfant Plaza SW, Room 4446, Washington, DC 20260-5015. Faxed comments aren't accepted, and on October 19 regulations.gov listed the document (USPS-2026-2511-0001) as not open for comment there.

entry.title: Verizon Lock Screen Rewards: $5/month for keeping "Do not sell or share" off so Glance can target ads
entry.summary: Verizon's privacy policy, now marked "Updated October 2026," adds a new paragraph: "Verizon Wireless customers participating in Verizon Dollars may be offered an opportunity to earn Verizon Dollars through use of the Glance lockscreen app." It goes on: "If you consent, Glance may collect, use and share personal information, including sensitive personal information, as described in the Glance AI privacy policy, for purposes such as delivering interest-based advertising." An Open Terms Archive capture first recorded the paragraph on the evening of October 16, 2026 (Mountain time), and the previous version didn't have it. The deal itself is spelled out in section 4, "Glance Lock screen Rewards," of the Verizon Dollars Program terms. Postpaid account owners and managers "may earn $5 in Verizon Dollars each calendar month by actively engaging with the Glance Platform for at least 60 minutes during that month." To qualify, you must grant and keep Glance location access, provide a selfie (or a gallery image or a stock avatar), keep "Do not sell or share my personal information" disabled (toggled off), keep "Limit use or disclosure of my sensitive personal information" disabled (toggled off), and keep "Enhanced browsing" on. On iPhone, you also need three Glance widgets on the Lock Screen and one on the Home Screen, and you can't select "Ask App Not to Track" for the Glance AI app. On Android, Glance must be your active lock screen with notification access. Section 10.2 says it plainly: "Glance requires you to share personal information, including sensitive personal information, which it uses to serve you personalized ads," and "If you stop sharing information with Glance or opt out of sale or sharing or targeted advertising with Glance, you will no longer qualify." Verizon calls the program a "financial incentive under California law" and a possible "bona fide loyalty program" under Colorado law. Those are the legal labels for paying people in exchange for their data. Verizon's FAQ adds that precise location should be set to "Only while using the app" and that you must "Grant permission to use your content for Glance AI features." The engagement timer runs only while you actively read, scroll, tap or ask the AI questions. It stops if you go idle, switch apps or turn on "Do not sell." The most you can earn is $60 a year. For anyone without a Verizon Visa Card, Verizon Dollars expire 12 months after they're issued and can't be used as a bill credit; they go toward gift cards, Verizon Store items and devices. The program terms page carries an effective date of June 16, 2026. We couldn't find an archived copy showing when the Glance section was added. To leave, uninstall Glance or delete your account in the Glance app settings. We found no news coverage of the program's data conditions.

entry.title: Evernote terms (Dec 1, 2026 for existing users): Italian affiliate, Brazil arbitration, no password-manager use
entry.summary: Evernote posted Terms of Service dated "Last update: October 1, 2026," replacing the January 1, 2026 version. An Evernote help article updated the same day says that if you signed up before October 1, 2026, the changes take effect on December 1, 2026; for everyone else they are already in force. The help article's main points: your contract transfers to Bending Spoons Operations S.p.A., an Italian company in Milan; legal terms now come in two versions (EEA/UK/Switzerland vs everywhere else, with Evernote Enterprise always on the second); Brazil users no longer contract with Evernote do Brasil or use Brazilian law, and instead get the non-EEA terms "including their governing law and arbitration agreement"; EEA/UK/Switzerland users get Italian law and no arbitration agreement; software license terms are folded into the Terms of Service; Evernote Points are no longer issued. The live Terms also add an AI clause: what you provide to AI features, and the results, are yours, and "We do not use what you provide to, or receive from, those features to train artificial intelligence models or tools." Buried in the conduct rules is a new ban that was not in the January 1, 2026 Terms: "you will not use the Evernote Service to back up your hard drive or to store or archive files" and "you will not use the Evernote Service as a password manager or to store sensitive financial information." The Terms also newly say Evernote "may use human and automated means to screen, monitor, and detect Content" that may be unlawful or violate the Terms. How it compares inside Evernote's own update (checked October 18, 2026 against the help article and live Terms): users in the EEA, UK, and Switzerland get Italian law and no arbitration agreement; Brazil users lose Evernote do Brasil / Brazilian law and instead get the non-EEA package "including their governing law and arbitration agreement." The live non-EEA Terms still include a 30-day arbitration opt-out: email optout@evernote.com within 30 days of first use after the arbitration agreement is introduced or updated (the opt-out section still refers to the February 15, 2024 Arbitration Agreement update). That window matters most for Brazilians who are newly under the arbitration clause on December 1. Coverage check October 18, ~3 PM MT: still no news articles; only Evernote's help page and our write-up.

entry.title: Roblox terms (Nov 1, 2026): Roblox is merchant of record for most purchases; parents must accept for kids
entry.summary: Roblox's Terms of Use now carry "Effective Date: November 1, 2026." A Roblox Support article and an Oct 1 Developer Forum post say the update simplifies wording, and clarifies that "Roblox acts as the principal distributor and merchant of record for purchases made through Roblox," so "when you access or purchase any content on the Roblox Platform, you are obtaining the content from Roblox" and "Users and Creators do not enter into a direct transaction with each other for those purchases," with related clarifications on Robux, payments, tax, and Creator payment. EEA users get a consumer right of withdrawal. The User Terms state that for U.S. and Canadian residents (except Quebec), disputes go through mandatory informal dispute resolution and then binding individual arbitration with a class action waiver; minors need a parent or legal guardian to accept the updated terms to keep using Roblox. The published terms also add a dedicated AI Features section: Outputs may be wrong, and creators' license to Roblox includes use "in connection with developing, improving, or training any AI or machine learning models" (language that already appeared in an earlier draft capture). Niche coverage: an Oct 8 blog post focused on a viral VPN-ban rumor; Roblox's own DevForum and Support pages are the primary sources. No major news outlet found covering the merchant-of-record change.

entry.title: Report, October 17, 2026
Google privacy policy (Oct 16, 2026): Gmail, Photos and Drive data shared with Search or Gemini can personalize ads
entry.summary: Google's privacy policy now reads "Effective October 16, 2026." It used to say flatly: "We don't show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos." That line now ends "unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads." A new passage says you "may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive," and that "Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads." Personalized ads are now described as based on "your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services." The policy also adds a definition tied to features such as "Personal Intelligence," with the example of Search using hotel booking details from an email to suggest things to do nearby. The access is opt-in: the policy frames it as something you choose to allow, subject to each service's own settings.

entry.title: GitHub: AI secret detection now covers push protection, billed by usage
entry.summary: In the GitHub Secret Protection section of GitHub's pricing page, the "Copilot secret scanning" row is renamed "AI detection for alerts" ("Use AI to detect unstructured secrets, like passwords, in existing code"). A new row, "AI detection for push protection," uses AI to "detect unstructured secrets, like passwords, and block pushes that contain them," and is listed as "Usage-based" rather than included in the plan price.

entry.title: Oura terms update (Nov 4, 2026): accept in the app or lose access; jury waiver and mass-arbitration batches added
entry.summary: Oura's Terms of Use now read "Last Updated: October 2, 2026" and "Effective Date: November 4, 2026," replacing the April 20, 2026 version. An Oura help-center article (last updated October 13) says members must accept the new terms in the Oura App by November 4: "After that date, you can't use the Oura App until you accept." The biggest rewrite is the U.S. dispute section. The old terms had one paragraph requiring arbitration and waiving class actions. The new Section XVI has 12 numbered parts. Disputes go to the American Arbitration Association (AAA), the provision "includes a class action and jury trial waiver," it covers any dispute "regardless of when it accrued," and it "supersedes all prior versions." Before filing, you must mail a written "Pre-Dispute Notice" to Oura's agent for service of process in Sacramento and negotiate for 30 days. Claims of $50,000 or less are decided on written submissions unless the arbitrator decides to hold a hearing. A new "Mass Arbitration Procedures" section applies when 25 or more similar claims are filed by people whose lawyers work together: 20 randomly picked cases go first, the rest are paused (with deadlines tolled) until those are decided and a mediation is held, then the next batch of 20 proceeds. Claims exempt from arbitration include small-claims cases, public injunctive relief under California law, and "any claim or cause of action for vexatious litigation." Neither version offers an arbitration opt-out. Other changes: the old promise to email you "at least thirty (30) days in advance" of a fee change is replaced by notice "in advance of the effective date and within the timeframe required by applicable law," plus a new right to cancel before a new fee applies. The liability cap changes from $100 to "the amount paid to Oura in the prior twelve (12) months." The old one-year deadline for filing claims is gone. Renewal charges move from one day before your billing anniversary to the anniversary itself, and you must cancel at least one day before renewal. The data section now says Oura "disclaims all liability that arises out of or in any way relates to any information that you provide or direct to be provided to Oura, even if that information constitutes electronic patient health records," and that Oura "may use, process, or share it, consistent with" the terms and its Privacy Policy. Oura says the update "does not change how Oura collects, uses, or protects member data," and its Privacy Policy is still dated June 15, 2026. The terms also add a "Regulated Features" section that names the Fertile Window feature in Cycle Insights as a medical device in the EU. How it compares (checked October 17, 2026): WHOOP's Terms of Use (last updated August 3, 2026) also require arbitration with a class action and jury trial waiver, but say "UNLESS YOU OPT OUT OF THE AGREEMENT TO ARBITRATE WITHIN 30 DAYS," and let members reject an updated agreement by emailing support@whoop.com within 30 days, keeping the prior terms until their current membership ends. Eight Sleep's Terms of Service (last updated September 16, 2026) say "YOU MAY OPT OUT OF ARBITRATION WITHIN 30 DAYS OF FIRST AGREEING TO THESE TERMS" by writing to legal@eightsleep.com. Oura's new terms offer no arbitration opt-out and no way to reject the update except to stop using the app ("your only recourse is to cease using the Services").

entry.title: Rocket Money bill negotiation moves to Premium+ ($15/month) on Nov 2, 2026; 35-60% success fee option ends
entry.summary: Rocket Money's Terms of Service now read "Effective 10/02/2026," replacing the June 29, 2026 version. The Bill Negotiation section adds: "As of November 2, 2026, Bill Negotiation is exclusively a Premium+ feature. Negotiations already in progress or on a payment plan will continue. Auto-renegotiations will sunset on November 2, 2026." Until now, members on other plans, including the free tier, could have Rocket Money negotiate a bill and pay only if it worked: a success fee "decided by the user, anywhere between 35-60% of the 12-month savings achieved." The terms' own example: at a 40% fee, a $10-a-month reduction costs $48. That pay-per-success option ends for negotiations started after November 2. Rocket Money's help center says Premium+ is "$15/month plus tax," that "there's no paid, a la carte option," and that Premium+ members can have one negotiation in progress at a time. Members who don't upgrade keep the rest of their plan but "won't be able to submit new Bill Negotiations after November 2." Automatic renegotiations, the ones Rocket Money scheduled through its TrueProtect feature, end November 1 according to the help center: "the one you had scheduled through TrueProtect won't happen," so you have to ask for each new negotiation yourself. At $15 a month, Premium+ costs $180 a year before tax, whether or not any bill gets lowered. The same terms update adds a "Conversation memory" clause for Rowan, Rocket Money's AI assistant, which "may retain summarized information from your conversations, such as your goals, preferences, and communication style," and a new section on reading Gmail content if you connect a Google account.

entry.title: Report, October 16, 2026
Cloudflare Pipelines is no longer free: Basin pricing is $0.04/GB transforms, $0.03-$0.06/GB delivery
entry.summary: Cloudflare's plans page used to list Pipelines ingestion and delivery to R2 as "TBD (free during beta)". It now shows real prices for the product, now part of the Cloudflare Basin family. Stream ingress is free and unlimited. SQL transforms include 50 GB a month, then $0.04 per GB. Sink delivery includes 50 GB a month shared across sinks, then $0.03 per GB for JSON or $0.06 per GB for Parquet or Iceberg. The page also adds catalog pricing (1 million operations a month included, then $9 per million; compaction at $0.005 per GB after 10 GB and $2 per million objects after 1 million) and query pricing (10 GB of compressed data scanned a month included, then $0.0025 per GB, which is $2.50 per TB, with a 10 MB minimum per query). R2 storage and operations are billed separately.

The regular annual Premium prices listed on the same page are unchanged at $149.50 a year for 12 credits and $229.50 a year for 24 credits, and monthly Premium is still $14.95. The page doesn't spell out the offer's terms or end date.

entry.title: Robinhood Class Action Service: auto-enrollment on Nov 18, 2026 and a 20% fee (how to opt out)
entry.summary: Robinhood's Customer Agreement (revised October 1, 2026) adds Section 36A, a "Class Action Service" whose terms take effect "on or after November 18, 2026." It reads: "Your Account is automatically enrolled in Robinhood's Class Action Service (the "Class Action Service"), unless you unenroll as described in this Section 36A." Robinhood and a third-party vendor will automatically file claims for you in securities class-action settlements involving stocks held in your account, and the RHF Fee Schedule sets the Class Action Service Fee at "20% of the class action settlement proceeds received on your behalf." Enrollment lets Robinhood appoint the vendor "as your agent and attorney-in-fact," binds you to the settlement's releases, and means "you cannot separately bring a lawsuit, at any time, against any named defendant" in a case where a claim was filed for you. You also can't submit your own claim form for that settlement. Robinhood says it will notify you before each filing. You get seven business days to exclude that case, and you can unenroll from the service at any time through the app or Robinhood Customer Service. The September 1, 2026 version of the agreement had no such section. Settlement administrators don't usually charge anything to file your own claim form, so staying enrolled by default costs you a fifth of any payout. Other brokers run similar auto-enrolled services, but the cut varies: E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley's vendor deducts 6% of payments (etrade.com class action terms), Edward Jones' administrator Broadridge deducts 15% (Edward Jones service disclosure), and Interactive Brokers charges a 20% contingency fee (IBKR Securities Class Action Recovery page), so Robinhood's 20% sits at the top of that range. Checked October 16, 2026.

entry.title: DoorDash terms update (Oct 16, 2026): arbitration now covers Stripe, Persona and other vendors; JAMS; robot deliveries
entry.summary: DoorDash's Consumer Terms and Conditions now read "Effective: October 16, 2026," replacing the August 13, 2026 version. The new text went live on Oct 16, after our early-morning check that day. A new "Related Third Parties" clause extends the arbitration agreement to disputes with DoorDash's "affiliates, subsidiaries, successors, related entities, agents, employees, contractors, subcontractors, insurers, licensees, assignees, vendors, and suppliers," and names "Amplitude, Persona, Checkr, Blue Star, Stripe, Payfare." All U.S. arbitrations move to JAMS. The old terms used ADR Services for California residents and National Arbitration and Mediation (NAM) for everyone else. The arbitration agreement now survives "until the expiration of all applicable statutes of limitations." Opting out of arbitration is still limited to new accounts, which must email opt-out@doordash.com within 30 days. Each opt-out notice must now come from you personally, not an agent, and can't cover more than one user. "Contractors" are renamed "Delivery Providers," a term that now covers "technology, including autonomous vehicles." A new "Autonomous Deliveries" section says DoorDash "may, in its sole discretion, utilize autonomous vehicles or other technology to facilitate deliveries." Some changes favor customers. U.S. orders are now governed by the law of the state where you live instead of Delaware law. The damages limits no longer cover death or bodily injury caused by DoorDash's own negligence, gross negligence or willful misconduct, sexual assault or harassment claims, or refunds of what you paid. The terms also add "Pay with Rewards" (paying with credit-card points) and rewrite the marketing-text section.

entry.title: Proton terms update (Oct 9, 2026): Proton can discontinue services or features with or without notice
entry.summary: Proton's Terms of Service now say "Last modified: October 09, 2026," replacing the June 23, 2026 version, and Section 4 ("Limited warranties and liability") opens differently. The old opening said Proton "does not make any warranty about the reliability of the Services or the security of user data, despite best efforts," and that the Service is provided "as is" and "as available." That paragraph is gone. In its place: "The Company reserves the right, at its sole discretion, to modify, suspend, or discontinue any of our Services, or any feature or component thereof, with or without notice to you." Proton says it "will endeavor to provide reasonable advance notice of a material discontinuation" where practicable, but "has no obligation to provide such notice, and is not liable to you or any third party" for any modification, suspension, or discontinuation, to the extent the law allows. The terms cover Proton Mail, Calendar, Drive, VPN, Pass, Meet, and Docs. Nothing else in the document changed, including the liability cap of $100 or the amount you paid.

entry.title: Report, October 15, 2026
Shopify raised annual prices: Grow now $89/mo, Advanced $359/mo (pricing update)
entry.summary: Shopify's pricing page now shows pay-yearly prices of $89/mo for Grow (was $79) and $359/mo for Advanced (was $299). That cuts the annual-billing discount from about 25% to about 15% on Grow and about 10% on Advanced, and raises a year of Grow from $948 to $1,068 and a year of Advanced from $3,588 to $4,308.

entry.title: Slack Enterprise+ price is now public: $45 per user per month (annual)
entry.summary: Slack's pricing page used to say "Contact sales for pricing" for Enterprise+. It now lists $45 USD per user per month when paying annually, with the Contact Sales button still shown.

entry.title: Claude Enterprise now requires 20 seats minimum (Anthropic pricing update)
entry.summary: The Enterprise plan on Anthropic's pricing page still reads US$20/seat/month billed annually plus usage at API rates, but now adds "20 seat minimum." That implies at least $4,800 a year in seat fees before any usage.

entry.title: Figma: New Figma Specs beta added to paid seats
entry.summary: Figma's pricing page adds Figma Specs, a beta for writing structured specs on the canvas, available on paid seats. Full, Dev, and Collab seat descriptions now all include Figma Specs, and Full seats now explicitly list Figma Motion. Figma Make also gains secrets management and a scaffolded Payload backend (database, APIs, auth, admin panel).

entry.title: Audible: Annual plans: cancellation now effective next billing cycle
entry.summary: Audible's plan page now says its annual Premium plans ($149.50/yr for 12 credits, $229.50/yr for 24 credits) can be canceled anytime "effective next billing cycle," where it previously just said "Cancel anytime." The "Save 16%" labels on the annual plans were also removed. Prices did not change.

entry.title: Bank of America's new online banking agreement limits disputes on linked external accounts (Oct 19, 2026)
entry.summary: Bank of America's new Online Banking Service Agreement takes effect October 19, 2026, replacing the August 27, 2026 version. The prior text gave customers 90 days to report errors or unauthorized activity "if the problem or error relates to a transfer from an account maintained at another financial institution." The new text keeps that 90-day window only for Bill Pay payments funded from an outside account to an outside, third-party payee. It adds: "Except for transfers initiated through the Bill Pay Service that are funded from an account maintained at another financial institution ('External Account')… Bank of America is not responsible for investigating or resolving errors or other disputes for electronic transactions that appear on your External Account statement." A related line says the unauthorized-transaction protections in Section 8.B "apply only to accounts maintained with Bank of America," with the same Bill Pay exception. Paying a BofA card or loan from a linked Chase or credit-union account now means taking most disputes to that other bank.

entry.title: Verizon Regulatory Charge rising to $0.26 per line on Nov 1, 2026 (and USF at a record 42%)
entry.summary: Verizon's surcharges support page now states: "Effective November 1, 2026, the monthly Verizon Wireless Regulatory Charge for voice-capable devices will increase from $0.21 to $0.26 per line." That is a 24% jump on one of Verizon's own mobile surcharges (not a government tax). Combined with the unchanged Administrative and Telco Recovery Charge ($3.78 per voice line), Verizon's two flat per-line surcharge lines go from $3.99 to $4.04. Separately, Verizon disclosures show the Federal Universal Service Charge using a 42% factor, matching the FCC's Q4 2026 contribution factor (DA-26-946), the program's highest on record after 38.8% in Q3.

entry.title: DOT delays airline "controllable delay" change to Feb 1, 2027: maintenance, medical, unruly-passenger delays
entry.summary: A Federal Register notice published October 15, 2026 (FR Doc 2026-21058) delays the effective date of DOT's September 3, 2026 final rule on airline delay and cancellation categories under Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act. The rule, which creates a new category for ten events that will no longer count as "Air Carrier" (controllable) delays or cancellations—including certain unscheduled maintenance, removing an unruly passenger, medical emergencies, cyberattacks, and government system failures—now takes effect February 1, 2027 instead of October 19, 2026. The new categories apply to flights on or after January 1, 2027, so holiday-season flights stay under the old categories. DOT's earlier analysis said the change is expected to reduce the number of delays and cancellations for which carriers provide amenities and compensation under voluntary commitments.

entry.title: Report, October 14, 2026
Cash App can now auto-sell your bitcoin to cover ACH debits (terms update)
entry.summary: Cash App’s terms now describe an optional feature that, when enabled, automatically sells Virtual Currency from your Hosted Balance at the then-effective Conversion Rate to cover eligible ACH debit payments from your Cash App Balance. You may not get a separate notice before each sale; bitcoin price can move between the debit request and the sale; and you can turn the feature off, though pending sales may still complete.

entry.title: Squarespace pricing now lists AI credits by plan, and Basic's 2% store fee
entry.summary: The Squarespace pricing page now lists AI credit allotments by plan (Basic: 10 one-time; Core: 20/mo; Plus: 40/mo) and shows a 2% online store transaction fee on Basic, while Core and above advertise no online-store transaction fees. Listed plan prices ($25 / $39 / $65 / $139) and card rates were unchanged in the snapshot.

entry.title: Report, October 13, 2026
